Bias of Pearson's correlation coefficient under contamination

Source: R/utils_impact.R
bias.Rd

Compute the bias of Pearson's correlation functional at a contaminated distribution \(F_\varepsilon = (1 - \varepsilon) F + \varepsilon H\), where \(F\) is the model distribution, \(H\) is the contamination distribution, and \(\varepsilon \in [0, 0.5)\) is the contamination fraction.

bias(model, epsilon, contamination = "careless", ...)

Arguments

model

list of relevant quantities detailing the distribution of ordinal measurement scales, as generated by [get_model()] or [simple_model()].

epsilon

vector of contamination fractions. Its elements must be between 0 and 0.5.

contamination

the type of contamination. Possible values are: - `"careless"`: contamination distribution corresponding to (stylized) careless responding behavior, as generated by [careless()]. - `"reversed"`: contamination distribution corresponding to respondents reversing one or both scales in a model distribution, as generated by [reversed()]. - `"adversarial"`: adversarial contamination distribution resulting in maximum upward or downward bias, as generated by [adversarial()].

...

additional arguments to be passed to the corresponding function generating the relevant quantities of the contamination distribution.

Value

A list with the following components:

epsilon

vector of contamination fractions.

rho

true correlation coefficient at the model distribution.

rho_contaminated

vector containing the correlation coefficient at the contaminated distribution for each contamination fraction.

bias

vector containing the bias of the correlation at the contaminated distribution for each contamination fraction.

References

M. Welz, A. Archimbaud, A. Alfons (2026). Quantifying the impact of careless responding. PsyArXiv. doi:10.31234/osf.io/8fj6p_v2 .

See also

[get_model()], [simple_model()]

[careless()], [reversed()], [adversarial()]

Author

Andreas Alfons and Max Welz

Examples

# generate model distribution
model_XY <- simple_model(prob = "centered", K = 9,
                         length = 5, rho_w = 0.4,
                         rho = -0.4)

# contamination fractions
eps <- c(0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.49)

# straightlining from extreme response categories
bias(model_XY, epsilon = eps, contamination = "careless",
     type = "straightlining", target = "extreme")
#> $epsilon
#> [1] 0.00 0.10 0.20 0.30 0.40 0.49
#> 
#> $rho
#> [1] -0.4
#> 
#> $rho_contaminated
#> [1] -0.4000000  0.3121809  0.5795408  0.7196501  0.8058929  0.8593435
#> 
#> $bias
#> [1] 0.0000000 0.7121809 0.9795408 1.1196501 1.2058929 1.2593435
#> 


# straightlining from all response categories
bias(model_XY, epsilon = eps, contamination = "careless",
     type = "straightlining", target = "all")
#> $epsilon
#> [1] 0.00 0.10 0.20 0.30 0.40 0.49
#> 
#> $rho
#> [1] -0.4
#> 
#> $rho_contaminated
#> [1] -0.40000000  0.02195337  0.28959445  0.47448755  0.60987001  0.70405156
#> 
#> $bias
#> [1] 0.0000000 0.4219534 0.6895944 0.8744875 1.0098700 1.1040516
#> 

# random responding from extreme response categories
bias(model_XY, epsilon = eps, contamination = "careless",
     type = "random", target = "extreme")
#> $epsilon
#> [1] 0.00 0.10 0.20 0.30 0.40 0.49
#> 
#> $rho
#> [1] -0.4
#> 
#> $rho_contaminated
#> [1] -0.4000000 -0.3313772 -0.2728627 -0.2223764 -0.1783721 -0.1433350
#> 
#> $bias
#> [1] 0.00000000 0.06862284 0.12713727 0.17762357 0.22162787 0.25666503
#> 

# random responding from all response categories
bias(model_XY, epsilon = eps, contamination = "careless",
     type = "random", target = "all")
#> $epsilon
#> [1] 0.00 0.10 0.20 0.30 0.40 0.49
#> 
#> $rho
#> [1] -0.4
#> 
#> $rho_contaminated
#> [1] -0.4000000 -0.3682275 -0.3349688 -0.3001171 -0.2635550 -0.2290805
#> 
#> $bias
#> [1] 0.00000000 0.03177248 0.06503120 0.09988294 0.13644495 0.17091946
#>
